terms.grammar: pronoun (possessive), first and second declension; vocative masculine mī
terms.comment: Agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. “Mine” is the same word used as a predicate: meum est, it’s mine. Latin leaves the possessive out where the owner is plain from the context (see your); put it in for stress or contrast, and before its noun for weight. In address, mī pater, mea Tullia. For “my own” see own.

phrases.latin: quae tua sunt, tibi habē: quae mea, redde mihi
phrases.english: What is yours, keep for yourself; what is mine, give back to me.
“All my goods,” he says, “are with me.”

phrases.latin: Quid agitur, Aeschine? — Ehem, pater mī, tū hīc erās?
phrases.english: How are you, Aeschinus? — Oh, my father, you were here?

phrases.latin: ibi mihi Tulliola mea fuit praestō nātālī suō ipsō diē
phrases.english: There my little Tullia was waiting for me, on her very birthday.

phrases.latin: cūr ego tēcum nōn sum? cūr ocellōs Ītaliae, vīllulās meās, nōn videō?
phrases.english: Why am I not with you? Why can’t I see my little country houses, the eyes of Italy?
